source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning Code Generation with Large Language Models
finding: Model first writes a short step plan from the request, then writes code from it. Beats direct and chain-of-thought code generation. This is plan-then-implement done by a model.
numbers: code-davinci-002, Pass@1 HumanEval: Direct 48.1, Few-shot 52.6, Code CoT 53.9, Self-planning 60.3 (+25.4% relative to Direct, +11.9% over CoT). MBPP-sanitized Pass@1: Direct 49.8, Few-shot 53.5, CoT 54.5, Self-planning 55.7.
limits: Old model, greedy decoding, one run. Gain over few-shot on MBPP is only about 2 points.
agent_relevance: Plan-first is a cheap measured gain, but small on easy problems.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning Code Generation with Large Language Models
finding: Quality of the plan is the bottleneck: giving the model a human-quality (ground-truth) plan raises accuracy far more than self-made plans.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1: self-plan 60.3 vs ground-truth plan 74.4 (+54.7% over Direct). MBPP-sanitized: 55.7 vs 65.1 (+30.7%).
limits: Ground-truth plans were derived from reference code, so they leak the solution shape.
agent_relevance: Most of the upside is in getting the plan right, so plan checking matters more than plan writing.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning Code Generation with Large Language Models
finding: Planning helps more on harder problems. Splitting HumanEval by complexity, the gain grows with difficulty.
numbers: Pass@1 Direct / CoT / Self-planning: Complexity 1 65.2 / 68.1 / 71.2; Complexity 2 36.2 / 44.7 / 55.3 (+52.7% over Direct); Complexity 3 31.1 / 37.3 / 50.2 (+61.5%).
limits: Complexity buckets are the authors' own; small buckets.
agent_relevance: Use a plan phase when a problem has several parts; skip it on trivial items.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning Code Generation with Large Language Models
finding: How the plan is delivered matters. Plan and code as separate single-turn phases works; a multi-turn dialogue version collapses.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1: multi-turn 28.2, one-phase 62.8, two-phase 60.3. Few-shot count: 1-shot 53.2, 2-shot 54.8, 4-shot 59.0. Zero-shot CoT one phase 18.0 vs two-phase 50.6.
limits: Single model, one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Keep plan and code as slots the program controls, not a free chat. Matches our rule that code decides transitions.

source: Li et al. (2023) Structured Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Code Generation
finding: Reasoning steps written with the three program structures (sequence, branch, loop) plus input-output, instead of free prose. A small fixed vocabulary of plan parts.
numbers: ChatGPT Pass@1: HumanEval CoT 53.29 vs SCoT 60.64 (+13.79%); MBPP 41.83 vs 46.98 (+12.31%); MBCPP 53.51 vs 57.06 (+6.63%). Codex HumanEval 43.79 vs 49.82 (+13.77%). Zero-shot ChatGPT HumanEval 49.73.
limits: Gains shrink at Pass@5 (HumanEval +2.38%). Two LLMs only.
agent_relevance: A structured step vocabulary beats free text for code tasks.

source: Li et al. (2023) Structured Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Code Generation
finding: Ablation: removing the loop/branch/sequence structure hurts more than removing the input-output line. Pseudocode as the intermediate is worse than SCoT.
numbers: ChatGPT HumanEval Pass@1: full SCoT 60.64; without basic structures 55.67; without IO structure 59.65; SCoT-P (pseudocode) 55.23; CoT 53.29. Example seeds A/B/C SCoT 60.64/60.27/59.36 vs CoT 53.29/52.81/51.36; three annotators SCoT 59.48 to 60.64.
limits: One model, one benchmark for the ablation; the structure names are the authors' choice.
agent_relevance: Name control-flow shape explicitly in the plan. Result is robust to who writes the examples.

source: Zelikman et al. (2023) Parsel: Algorithmic Reasoning with Language Models by Composing Decompositions
finding: Plan is a tree of function descriptions. Model writes several implementations per function; code runs tests and picks a combination that passes. Plan composition with solved subgoals checked by code.
numbers: APPS competition-level: direct Codex/AlphaCode pass rate 14.5% vs Parsel 25.5% (pass@8x16). HumanEval with GPT-4: 67% to 85.1% with generated tests; pass@any 91.5% with 8 Parsel programs vs 82.3% with 64 direct; 93.9% (16x8) vs 84.1% (128 direct).
limits: Needs tests per function; test quality sets the ceiling. Ablation used 100 sampled problems.
agent_relevance: Closest working match to our design: decompose, solve parts, let code compose and verify.

source: Zelikman et al. (2023) Parsel: Algorithmic Reasoning with Language Models by Composing Decompositions
finding: Ablation: the plan alone does not give the gain. Same high-level plans translated straight to Python (no compose-and-test step) lose almost everything.
numbers: Same budget, 100 APPS problems: full pipeline pass@8x16 25.5% vs direct Python from the plan 6%; problems solved without Parsel were a strict subset of those solved with it. Pass rate rose log-linearly with number of evaluations. A 2.7B CodeGen solved none.
limits: Codex-era result; small models solved nothing.
agent_relevance: The check-and-recombine step, not the plan text, carries the gain. Supports G3 (verify on held-out tests).

source: Le et al. (2024) CodeChain: Towards Modular Code Generation through Chain of Self-Revisions with Representative Sub-Modules
finding: Model writes modular code, sub-modules are clustered, cluster representatives are fed back as reusable parts for the next round. A direct test of reusing solved subgoals.
numbers: APPS Pass@1 all: GPT-3.5 22.33 to CodeChain 30.24 (about +35% relative); competition level 5.42 to 12.38; interview 19.42 to 28.11. WizardCoder 7.90 to 10.50. With CodeT filtering 32.54 to 35.34. CodeContests: +76% relative.
limits: Gain small for the open model.
agent_relevance: Reusing representative modules is a measured gain; recall picked by clustering.

source: Le et al. (2024) CodeChain: Towards Modular Code Generation through Chain of Self-Revisions with Representative Sub-Modules
finding: Ablation on what to feed back: sub-modules chosen by cluster centroid beat whole programs, and centroid beats random.
numbers: APPS validation Pass@1, GPT-3.5, one revision round, with CoT prompting and public-test filtering: random whole program 30.16, centroid whole program 32.87, centroid sub-modules 35.11 (best row).
limits: Validation subset; table text was partly garbled in extraction, so row labels were read with the paper prose.
agent_relevance: Pick stored parts by representativeness, not at random.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Search over many different natural-language plans, not over many code samples. Plans give diversity that repeated code sampling lacks.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, Claude 3.5 Sonnet: pass@1 without search 41.4%; repeated sampling pass@200 60.6%; PlanSearch pass@200 77.0%.
limits: Needs about 200 samples and a pass oracle for pass@k.
agent_relevance: Plan diversity is where search budget should go. G4 still applies: samples from one model are correlated.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: A correct plan is nearly sufficient: a back-translated correct sketch, even about 10 tokens, raises accuracy a lot, and the solve rate given a sketch is bimodal (near 0% or near 100%).
numbers: GPT-4o-mini on LiveCodeBench: solve rates given a sketch polarize to 0% or 100%; most variance is whether the idea is right. Idea-diversity score correlates strongly with search gain across models, methods and benchmarks (Figure 6).
limits: Back-translated sketches come from known passing code, so this is an oracle upper bound.
agent_relevance: Errors are mostly wrong plan, not wrong coding. Spend checks on the plan step.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions
finding: Learns a library of reusable helper functions by refactoring solved programs and checking outputs are unchanged. Programs predicted with the library are more accurate.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B absolute gains: LOGO +11.5%, Date understanding +26.1%, TextCraft +8.1%; beats GPT-3.5 without library by 19.2% on LOGO. TextCraft CodeLlama-34B 22.2 to 30.8. Random curriculum instead of ordered: 18.7% drop on LOGO.
limits: About 200 training examples; wrong abstractions can hurt; needs execution checks.
agent_relevance: A solved-subgoal library helps, and learning order (easy to hard) matters.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
finding: LLM writes programs, a symbolic compressor (Stitch) extracts shared abstractions, and an LLM names and documents them. Compared with DreamCoder.
numbers: Online synthesis mean tasks solved: REGEX DreamCoder 43.93 vs LILO 77.07 (+33.14); LOGO 28.53 vs 48.95 (+20.42); CLEVR 94.50 vs 96.76 (+2.26). Best single run REGEX 93.20 vs 45.60.
limits: Three small DSL domains, 3 seeds; some LILO variants without AutoDoc scored lower.
agent_relevance: A stored subgoal needs a readable label (AutoDoc) for the model to reuse it.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: Older AI system that builds a library of reusable program parts (learns map, fold, filter) and uses it to solve harder problems. The machine version of a plan library.
numbers: SyGuS text editing, 108 problems: before learning 3.7% solved in 10 minutes (235 s average); after learning 79.6% (40 s average). Best competition solver CVC4 82.4% at 1 hour and 8 CPUs; DreamCoder 84.3% at the same budget.
limits: Domain-specific languages and search, no language model. I read the intro and results sections only.
agent_relevance: Library learning lifted solve rate from near zero and cut time about 6 times: stored parts are the lever.

source: Demirtas et al. (2025) Generating Planning Feedback for Open-Ended Programming Exercises with LLMs
finding: Tests whether LLMs can detect which programming plans a student program contains, even when the code is wrong. A modern test of Soloway-style plan recognition.
numbers: 1616 student submissions, human-labelled. Micro-F1: AST-rules 0.588, CodeBERT-kNN 0.550, GPT-4o prompted 0.778, GPT-4o-mini prompted 0.672, fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini 0.782, fine-tuned GPT-4o 0.771. Exact match: AST 0.526, GPT-4o 0.716.
limits: One CS1 course for non-majors and one plan set. Models over-predicted a plan instead of UNKNOWN.
agent_relevance: Models recognise plans in broken code far better than rule-based parsers; usable as a plan-detection slot.

source: Demirtas et al. (2025) Generating Planning Feedback for Open-Ended Programming Exercises with LLMs
finding: Plan recognition degrades gracefully with errors for LLMs but collapses for rule-based tools. Students who used the instructor's plans passed more often.
numbers: Micro-F1 on submissions with syntax errors: AST-rules 0.178, kNN 0.456, GPT-4o 0.726, GPT-4o-mini 0.531, tuned mini 0.694. Using instructor-set plans: 77.17% of fully passing submissions vs 61.40% of no-test-passing. No known plan: 4.62% of passers vs 18.80% of compile-error submissions.
limits: Association, not cause. Annotator agreement 90% on correct code, 66% on partly correct.
agent_relevance: Plan choice predicts success. A 'right plan chosen' check could gate attempts before running them.

source: Fisler, Krishnamurthi and Siegmund (2016) Modernizing Plan-Composition Studies
finding: Human background: argues plan-composition studies are dated and redesigns tasks (noisy data processing; students also evaluate programs) across functional and imperative courses.
numbers: Preliminary study in five courses, three functional and two imperative.
limits: No LLM involved. I found no standard LLM replication of Rainfall-style plan-composition tasks in this pass.
agent_relevance: A Rainfall-style task set for models appears missing; our own test would be new.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: An LLM agent loop that stores each verified solved subgoal as code in a skill library and retrieves it later. Solved-subgoal memory inside an agent.
numbers: Tech-tree iterations (mean +- sd): wooden tool Voyager 6+-2 vs AutoGPT 92+-72; stone 11+-2 vs 94+-72; iron 21+-7 vs 135+-103; diamond reached only by Voyager (1 of 3 runs, 102). ReAct and Reflexion 0/3 at every level. 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distance.
limits: Minecraft only. Without the library the early speed is similar (iron 29+-11 vs 21+-7).
agent_relevance: The library matters most for later, harder goals.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: Ablation: without the skill library progress plateaus in later stages; a random curriculum cuts item count sharply. Skills are committed only after the environment confirms success.
numbers: Without skill library: wooden 7+-2, stone 9+-4, iron 29+-11, diamond 0/3. Random curriculum: unique items drop 93%.
limits: The check is a game-state test, not general.
agent_relevance: Store a subgoal only after a code-checked pass (G2, G3).

source: Islam et al. (2024) MapCoder: Multi-Agent Code Generation for Competitive Problem Solving
finding: Four roles copying a human developer: recall similar solved problems, make a plan, write code, debug using the plan. Agent-loop use of schema retrieval plus planning.
numbers: Gain over direct prompting on competition sets: ChatGPT +41.3% APPS, +52.6% xCodeEval, +132.8% CodeContests; GPT-4 +73.7%, +41.2%, +135.1%. HumanEval ChatGPT full pipeline 80.0%. Ablation: dropping debugging alone loses 17.5 points; planning agent second most important (avg drop 16.7); average drop over all removals 24.83.
limits: Roles are prompts of one model; recall quality not measured on its own. Mistral-7B +111% on HumanEval from a low base (27.3%).
agent_relevance: Planning and plan-guided debugging each contribute.

source: Lei et al. (2025) Planning-Driven Programming: A Large Language Model Programming Workflow (LPW)
finding: The plan is checked against visible tests first (plan verification), and the verified plan then guides repair when code fails. I read the abstract and method sections only.
numbers: GPT-4o Pass@1: HumanEval 98.2%, MBPP 84.8%, LiveCode 59.3%, APPS 62.6%, CodeContests 34.7%; up to +16.4% over earlier methods.
limits: Uses visible tests; baselines as reported by the authors.
agent_relevance: Checking the plan on examples before coding fits our check-before-commit rule.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Skills-in-Context Prompting: Unlocking Compositionality in Large Language Models
finding: Put the basic skills and a worked composition of them in the same prompt. Models then compose skills on harder unseen problems.
numbers: ChatGPT dynamic programming (8 numbers) CoT 72.0 vs SKiC 98.0; last-letter concatenation (12 words) CoT 72.5 vs 100.0; GSM8K by exemplar order CoT 73.0 to 74.4 vs SKiC 86.9 to 87.8. Near-perfect generalization on addition, last-letter and DP with several models.
limits: Synthetic task families; MATH gain smaller (ChatGPT 40.6 with skills).
agent_relevance: Show the parts and one composition together: a cheap scaffold for plan composition.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
finding: Models solve compositional tasks by matching memorised sub-patterns, not by composing steps reliably. Accuracy falls toward zero as the composition graph grows.
numbers: Zero- and few-shot accuracy falls from near perfect to near zero with problem size on multiplication, logic grid puzzles and DP. For 4-digit by 2-digit multiplication, 82.3% of correct final answers had at least one error in the computation graph.
limits: GPT-3, ChatGPT, GPT-4 era; later reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Composing many small plans can silently break; step-level code checks are needed (G1, G3).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Stores high-level thought templates (schemas) distilled from solved problems, retrieves one and fills it in on a new problem. Schema retrieval in an LLM loop. I read the abstract and introduction only.
numbers: Reported gains over previous best: +11% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One; about 12% of the cost of tree/graph-of-thought on average.
limits: Authors' own runs on 10 tasks; templates built by the same model.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a reusable-schema buffer cuts cost; independence of evidence is weak.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows from its own past successful runs and gives them back as guidance. Solved-subgoal memory measured on web tasks.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): BrowserGym 23.5% to AWM 35.5% (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative); 7.6% relative above human-written workflows (SteP); about 2.0 fewer steps per task. Mind2Web +24.6% relative. Gap over baseline grows from 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test distance widens.
limits: Wrong induced workflows can degrade performance (authors note); success is judged by an automatic evaluator.
agent_relevance: Store workflows only from verified success; benefit grows as tasks drift.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Plan is split further only when the executor fails on a step (as-needed decomposition), not up front. I read the abstract and introduction only.
numbers: Success above strong baselines by up to 28.3% (ALFWorld), 27% (WebShop), 33% (TextCraft), absolute points.
limits: Decomposition trigger is executor failure, a signal the program can see.
agent_relevance: Direct match to G1: decompose on a failure signal, not on a schedule.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: After a plan fails, repair is limited by the model's feedback on its own code, not by its coding. Human feedback is far better than GPT-4 feedback.
numbers: Repair success with GPT-4 feedback vs human feedback: introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%; overall 33.30% vs 52.60%. At equal sample budget, gains from self-repair are often marginal or absent.
limits: Small human study; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama only.
agent_relevance: Revise from real failing output, not model opinion (G2); do not expect self-critique to fix a wrong plan.
